title: When, while and then
intro: This unit links actions and times. `-AndA` means **when**: *öýe gelende*, when I come home. `-kA` means **while** or **when … was**: *çagakam*, when I was a child. `-(Y)p` joins two actions in one sentence: *Bazara baryp, çörek aldym*, I went to the market and bought bread. Then four verbs of the body, *otyr*, *dur*, *ýatyr* and *ýör*, say what is going on right now, and a few words put a story in order: *ilki*, *ondan soň*, *iň soňunda*.

blocks.text: To say **when** something happens, add `-An` and the locative `-dA` to the verb stem: *gel-* → *gelende*, when (someone) comes; *bar-* → *baranda*, when (someone) goes there. The clause with `-AndA` comes first, and the verb at the end of the sentence gives the tense and the person.

After a vowel `-An` is just *-n*: *okanda*, *başlanda*. A final *e* becomes *ä*: *işle-* → *işlände*. The verbs that soften *t* before a vowel ([A1 unit 6](a1-u06)) do it here too: *gidende*, *edende*, *aýdanda*. For **when … not**, put `-mA` first: *gelmände*, when (someone) doesn't come.

`-AndA` has no tense of its own: the main verb decides. *Öýe gelende, çaý içýärin*, when I come home, I drink tea; *Öýe gelende, çaý içdim*, when I came home, I drank tea; *Öýe baranda, maňa jaň et*, call me when you get home.

**Who?** Say the subject at the start: *Men öýe gelende*, when I came home; *Ol gelende*, when he came. You will also see the endings of **my**, **your** before `-dA`, which say who without a pronoun: *gelenimde*, when I came; *geleniňde*, when you came; *gelenimizde*, when we came. Both are correct; this course practises the plain form and accepts both.

items.en: Call me when you get home.
When I got to Ashgabat, the weather was hot.
When I came to Turkmenistan, it was winter.

items.tk: Ol gelmände, men oňa jaň etdim.
items.seg: Ol gel|mä|n|de, men o|ň|a jaň et|di|m.
items.en: When he didn't come, I called him.

items.tk: Her gezek öýe gelende, kakama kömek edýärin.
items.seg: Her gezek öý|e gel|en|de, kaka|m|a kömek ed|ýär|in.
items.en: Every time I come home, I help my father.

blocks.title: The tense goes at the end
blocks.text: Only the main verb shows the tense: *Öýe gelende, çaý içdim*. Don't put the past on the `-AndA` verb: *gelende*, not `geldende`.

`-kA` (*-ka* or *-kä*) means **while** or **at the time when** something is so. It goes on a noun, an adjective or a place word, written as one word with it: *talyp* → *talypkam*, when I was a student; *gyzgyn* → *gyzgynka*, while (it is) hot; *öýde* → *öýdekä*, while (someone) is at home.

**Endings.** For **I** add *-m*, for **you** *-ň*, and for **he**, **she** or **it** nothing: *çagakam*, when I was a child; *çagakaň*, when you were a child; *çagaka*, when he or she was a child. These are short endings, like those of **my** and **your**.

**After `-ýAr`** it means **while (doing)**, **on the way**: *Men işden öýe gelýärkäm, dükana sowuldym*, on my way home from work, I stopped at the shop. Like `-AndA`, `-kA` has no tense: the main verb gives it.

items.en: When I was a child, I lived in a village.
When I was a student, I read a lot of books.
Drink the tea while it's hot!
On my way back from work, I stopped at the shop.
Let's head home while it's light.

blocks.title: When I was a child
blocks.text: English needs **when** and **was**; Turkmen needs one ending: *çagakam*. You will also hear *çaga wagtym*, literally **my child time**, for the same thing.

blocks.title: One word, and not -AndA
blocks.text: `-kA` is written onto its word: *çagakam*, not `çaga kam`. And it is not `-AndA`: *gelende* is **when (someone) comes**, *gelýärkä* is **while (someone) is coming**.

You know the converb `-(Y)p` from *ýüzüp bilýärin* ([A2 unit 5](a2-u05)). On its own, it joins actions done by the same person, one after the other: *Bazara baryp, çörek aldym*, I went to the market and bought bread. Only the last verb shows the tense and the person; the verbs in `-(Y)p` before it share them.

The spelling is that of [A2 unit 5](a2-u05): *-yp*, *-ip* after a consonant (*alyp*, *gelip*), *-up*, *-üp* after a rounded vowel in one syllable (*turup*, *gülüp*), *-p* after a vowel (*okap*), with *e* → *ä* (*işläp*) and the softened *t* (*gidip*, *edip*). A comma usually follows.

This is the usual way to tell actions in order, much more than *we*, and: *Ir turup, ýuwunyp, geýinip, çaý içdim*, I got up early, washed, got dressed and had tea. The tense of the last verb counts for all of them: *Ir turup, çaý içýärin*, I get up early and have tea.

items.en: I went to the market and bought bread.
He came home and ate.
I washed my hands and sat down to eat.
I crossed the street and went into the shop.

items.tk: Men ertir Mara gidip, kakamy görjek.
items.seg: Men ertir Mar|a gid|ip, kaka|m|y gör|jek.
items.en: Tomorrow I'll go to Mary and see my father.

blocks.title: Same subject only
blocks.text: `-(Y)p` joins actions of one subject. When two people act, give each a full verb: *Men geldim, Aýna gitdi*, I came and Aýna left.

sections.title: Going on now: otyr, dur, ýatyr, ýör

blocks.text: Four verbs describe how the body is: *oturmak*, to sit; *durmak*, to stand; *ýatmak*, to lie; *ýöremek*, to walk. Besides their usual forms, they have a present of their own for what is going on right now: *otyr*, (someone) is sitting; *dur*, is standing; *ýatyr*, is lying; *ýör*, is walking, going about. Their endings are those of `-ýAr`.

blocks.title: *oturmak*, its own present: I am sitting…

blocks.text: Where English just says **is**, Turkmen often names the posture: *Ejäm aşhanada otyr*, my mother is (sitting) in the kitchen; *Awtobus duralgada dur*, the bus is (standing) at the stop; *Jigim ýatakda ýatyr*, my little brother is lying in bed.

**The progressive.** After a verb in `-(Y)p`, the same four forms say that something is going on: *Ol kitap okap otyr*, she is reading a book; *Biz garaşyp otyrys*, we are waiting; *Çaga uklap ýatyr*, the child is sleeping; *Men Aşgabatda işläp ýörün*, I'm working in Ashgabat (these days). The first verb never changes; the helper takes the person.
**Which helper?** Partly the posture, partly the kind of action:

items: *otyr*: what someone is busy with right now, often sitting: *Näme edip otyrsyň?*, what are you doing?
*dur*: something seen going on, often brief or standing; also the weather: *Ýagyş ýagyp dur*, it's raining.
*ýatyr*: lying down, or a state that lasts: *uklap ýatyr*, is sleeping; *dynç alyp ýatyr*, is resting.
*ýör*: a longer stretch of time, these days, or moving about: *Ol heniz okap ýör*, she is still studying; *Olar gezip ýörler*, they are out walking.

blocks.text: When unsure, `-ýAr` is always right: *Ol kitap okaýar* also means she is reading a book. The progressive paints the picture. **Questions** take `-mY` at the end, as with `-ýAr`: *Näme edip otyrsyň?*, *Çaga uklap ýatyrmy?* For **not**, use the negative of `-ýAr`: *Ol häzir uklamaýar*, he isn't sleeping now.

items.en: She is reading a book.
We are waiting.
It's raining.
The child is sleeping.
I'm working in Ashgabat these days.
What are you doing?

blocks.title: The helper's own present
blocks.text: For **now**, the helper takes its own present: *okap otyryn*, *garaşyp durun*. The main verb stays in `-(Y)p` and never takes the person: not `okaýaryn otyr`.

sections.title: First, then, finally: telling a story

blocks.text: A few words put actions in order. You know *ilki*, first, and *soňra*, then, later ([A2 unit 7](a2-u07)). Add *ondan soň*, after that, and *iň soňunda*, in the end, finally. For reasons and results you have *sebäbi*, because, and *şonuň üçin*, so, that's why ([A1 unit 12](a1-u12)). *şeýle-de bolsa* means **however, even so**.

*ondan soň* is *ol* in the ablative, *ondan*, with *soň*: **after that** ([A2 unit 9](a2-u09)). *şeýle-de bolsa* is written with a hyphen and goes at the start of its sentence, followed by a comma. With `-(Y)p` these words make a whole story out of a few sentences.

items.en: First I went to the market and bought meat.

items.tk: Ondan soň öýe gelip, nahar bişirdim.
items.seg: O|n|dan soň öý|e gel|ip, nahar bişir|di|m.
items.en: After that I came home and cooked.
In the end the guests came.

items.tk: Nahar gowy däldi. Şeýle-de bolsa, hemme iýdi.
items.seg: Nahar gowy däl|di. Şeýle-de bolsa, hemme iý|di.
items.en: The food wasn't good. Even so, everyone ate.
I was late because the bus didn't come.

blocks.title: A day in four lines
blocks.text: *Ir turup, çaý içdim. Soňra işe gitdim. Ondan soň dostum bilen görüşdim. Iň soňunda öýe gaýtdym.* Read it again and spot each `-(Y)p` and each word of order.

summary: `-AndA` means **when**: *gelende*, *baranda*, *işlände*, *gidende*; the main verb gives the tense; *gelenimde* says **when I** with an ending.
`-kA` means **while** or **when … was**: *çagakam*, *talypkam*, *gyzgynka*, *öýdekä*; after `-ýAr`, *gelýärkäm*, on my way.
`-(Y)p` joins actions of one subject; only the last verb has the tense and the person: *Bazara baryp, çörek aldym*.
*otyr*, *dur*, *ýatyr*, *ýör* are the present of the posture verbs: *Ejäm aşhanada otyr*, *Awtobus duralgada dur*.
After `-(Y)p` they make the progressive: *okap otyr*, *ýagyp dur*, *uklap ýatyr*, *işläp ýörün*. `-ýAr` is always right too; for **not**, use the negative of `-ýAr`.
*ilki*, *soňra*, *ondan soň*, *iň soňunda* order a story; *sebäbi*, *şonuň üçin*, *şeýle-de bolsa* link the reasons.
